newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian coffee chief unveils austerity measures.
newsitem.headline: Colombian coffee chief unveils austerity measures.

text.p: Colombia's financially-troubled National Coffee Fund should save more than $180 million next year by slashing prices for growers and reducing overall spending, Jorge Cardenas, the head of the National Coffee Growers' Federation said.
He announced the austerity measures -- which could fuel mounting guerrilla violence in Colombia's central coffee-growing region -- at the end of a four-day annual meeting of coffee growers in Bogota.

The leading discussion item during the meeting was the financial crisis affecting the National Coffee Fund, the institution jointly administered by the government and Federation that pays Colombian coffee farmers for their crops.
Cardenas had warned in an address Wednesday that the fund was in such bad shape that it might not have enough money to buy Colombia's harvest in the 1997-98 coffee year.
Falling world prices, and a steep loss in export revenues due to the country's rapidly appreciating peso were expected to leave it with a $465 million deficit by next September, he said.

To help trim the deficit, Cardenas announced Thursday that authorities had agreed to cut Colombia's internal coffee price by 14,000 pesos per 125-kilo load, a move that he said would save the Coffee Fund about $70 million next year.

The internal price has held at 235,500 pesos since August, when it was raised from 201,500, and the cut is sure to draw protests from growers faced with with soaring production costs stemming from annual inflation of about 21 percent this year.
But Cardenas, who conceded that it was "difficult and painful," said it was necessary to pull the Coffee Fund up by its financial bootstraps. The price cut takes effect Friday.
Cardenas said an additional $113 million would be saved in 1997 through cuts in spending programs backed by the Coffee Fund.

He did not elaborate on where the budget axe would fall, but the fund finances everything from scientific investigation to the building of schools, clinics and roads in Colombia's main coffee-growing areas.

That social spending has been credited for years with keeping political violence to a mimimum in Colombia's main coffee-growing provinces. But growers warned during the four-day meeting here that leftist guerrillas were making inroads in the area, and any sharp cut in spending could make matters worse.

"The (financial) crisis in the coffee-growing region could help multiply the number of guerrillas in those areas of the country where they still aren't present," Octavio Arizmendi, a leading grower from Colombia's violence-torn northwest province of Antioquia told reporters at the meeting this week.

He and others told reporters that growers could offset the guerrilla threat by arming themselves and forming "self-defense" groups to patrol their plantations. But political analysts say paramilitaries have done far more to escalate Colombia's endemic violence that to stop it.
